passages.text: GEYSER, the name of the most remarkable of the boiling fountains of Iceland, situated in a plain near Skalholt.
The word is from the Icelandic geysa, to rage or gush.
At intervals it throws up a column of boiling water, with great noise, to the height of sixty feet and upwards, after which the water sinks again into the basin.
The heat of the water is ascribed to subterraneous fires, the same that feed the volcanoes of the island, and the force that throws it up to the elastic steam confined in caverns below.
The water deposits a white stony crust upon every thing it touches, so that leaves and moss dropped into it are in time turned to stone.
Such fountains are found in no other country so remarkable as in Iceland.

A geyser is a spring with an intermittent discharge of water ejected turbulently and accompanied by steam. Geysers are rare: they need water, a heat source and a particular underground plumbing system.
The term geyser comes from Geysir, the name of an erupting spring at Haukadalur, Iceland. That name comes from the Icelandic verb geysa, 'to gush'.

Groundwater is heated by hot rock above magma. In a narrow channel the water becomes superheated under pressure; when some of it boils, the pressure drops and the water column flashes to steam and erupts.
The erupted water carries dissolved silica, which is deposited around the vent as geyserite, also called siliceous sinter.
About 1,000 geysers exist worldwide, and about half of them are in Yellowstone National Park in the United States.
Earthquakes can start, change or stop geyser eruptions, as they have at the Great Geysir in Iceland.
Eruptions of nitrogen gas seen on Neptune's moon Triton in 1989 are described as cryogeysers.

reasons: Both explain the name from the Icelandic geysa.
The Geysir article scores close behind; it covers the single Icelandic spring the entry is about, so it is a second candidate.

alignments.label: The name

britannica.quote: from the Icelandic geysa, to rage or gush

alignments.note: Same word, same meaning. Wikipedia adds that one spring's name became the word for all of them.

alignments.label: The eruption

britannica.quote: At intervals it throws up a column of boiling water

wikipedia.quote: an intermittent discharge of water ejected turbulently and accompanied by steam

alignments.note: The same behaviour, in technical words.

alignments.label: Heat from below

britannica.quote: ascribed to subterraneous fires, the same that feed the volcanoes

wikipedia.quote: heated by hot rock above magma

alignments.note: Subterranean fire becomes magma. The link to volcanoes holds.

alignments.label: What drives it

britannica.quote: the elastic steam confined in caverns below

wikipedia.quote: the water column flashes to steam and erupts

alignments.note: Steam is the force in both. Wikipedia replaces a cavern of trapped steam with superheated water in a narrow channel.

alignments.label: Turned to stone

britannica.quote: deposits a white stony crust upon every thing it touches

wikipedia.quote: deposited around the vent as geyserite

alignments.note: The white crust is silica. It now has a name, geyserite.

alignments.label: Iceland the greatest

britannica.quote: found in no other country so remarkable as in Iceland

wikipedia.quote: about half of them are in Yellowstone National Park

alignments.note: True of the world Europeans knew in 1797. Inference: Yellowstone's geysers were not yet known to European science.

alignments.label: Earthquakes

wikipedia.quote: Earthquakes can start, change or stop geyser eruptions

alignments.note: The 1797 entry treats the Geyser as unchanging.

alignments.label: Beyond Earth

wikipedia.quote: Eruptions of nitrogen gas seen on Neptune's moon Triton

alignments.note: Neptune itself was found 49 years after this edition.

suggestedQuestions: How did the 1797 entry explain why the Geyser erupts?
Where does the word geyser come from?
Is Iceland still the most remarkable place for geysers?

How did the 1797 entry explain why the G.answer:
It said the water is heated by the same subterranean fires that feed Iceland's volcanoes, and thrown up by elastic steam confined in caverns below [B4]. Wikipedia agrees on the heat and on steam as the force: groundwater is heated by hot rock above magma, becomes superheated in a narrow channel, and flashes to steam [W3].

The difference is the plumbing: a narrow channel of superheated water, not a cavern of trapped steam.

Where does the word geyser come from?.answer: From the Icelandic geysa, 'to gush'; both texts agree [B2] [W2]. Wikipedia adds that the word came from Geysir, one spring at Haukadalur in Iceland [W2], which the 1797 entry describes as the most remarkable of the Icelandic fountains [B1].

Is Iceland still the most remarkable pla.answer: Not by number. The 1797 entry says no other country has such remarkable fountains [B6]. Wikipedia says about half of the world's roughly 1,000 geysers are in Yellowstone National Park [W5].
